entry: American defense and aerospace manufacturer, headquartered in North Bethesda, Maryland. It was formed by the merger of the Lockheed Corporation and Martin Marietta on March 15, 1995. As of 2023, it was the top contractor of the U.S. federal government; in 2024, 73% of its revenue came from the federal government, including 65% from the [[United States Department of Defense|Department of Defense]]. The F-35 fighter accounted for 26% of revenue that year. The company also manufactures the MIM-104 Patriot air-defense system and invests in [[Nuclear fusion|compact nuclear fusion]] and [[Renewable energy|renewable energy]] systems.

American family of single-seat, single-engine, supersonic stealth strike fighters. It is designed for air superiority and strike missions and also has electronic warfare and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities. [[Lockheed Martin]] is the prime contractor, with [[Northrop Grumman]] and BAE Systems as partners. It descends from the X-35, which beat the [[Boeing]] X-32 in 2001 to win the Joint Strike Fighter program. As of 2025, 883 aircraft were in service, making it the world's fourth-most-numerous military aircraft and its most-numerous stealth aircraft. The first combat use came in 2018, in [[Israel|Israeli]] strikes in [[Syria]]. Critics cite ballooning costs and delayed deliveries; the program is expected to cost US$2 trillion through 2088.

Long-range, high-altitude, Mach 3+ strategic reconnaissance aircraft. It was developed in the 1960s as a secret project and entered U.S. Air Force service in January 1966. Operating at Mach 3.2 and 85,000 feet (26,000 m), it could outrun a [[Surface-to-air missile|surface-to-air missile]] launch. From 1968 its missions flew from Okinawa over Laos and North Vietnam during the [[Vietnam War]], and later over North Korea. From 1976 it flew from RAF Mildenhall along Soviet Baltic and [[Barents Sea]] coastlines. Of 32 built, 12 were lost in accidents, none to enemy action. In 1974 it set the record for the quickest London–New York flight, and in 1976 it became the fastest airbreathing manned aircraft; as of 2026 it still holds both records. The U.S. Air Force retired it in 1989 and again in 1998, and [[NASA]] flew it for research until 1999.

Self-propelled railway vehicle that provides the motive power for a train, also called the engine of a train. Locomotives traditionally pulled trains from the front, but push–pull operation is now common, and longer freight trains use distributed power, with locomotives at the front, rear and intermediate points under the control of the leading unit. Locomotives draw power from fuel such as wood, coal, petroleum or natural gas, or from an outside source of electricity. The first full-scale working [[Steam locomotive|steam locomotive]] was built by Richard Trevithick in 1802. In 1812 Matthew Murray's Salamanca first ran and is generally regarded as the first commercially successful locomotive. [[George Stephenson]] built Locomotion No. 1 for the Stockton & Darlington Railway, the first public steam railway. Steam locomotives remained the most common type until after [[World War II]], when they were less efficient than diesel and electric types and needed larger crews.

Any of various short-horned grasshopper species, in the family Acrididae, that have a swarming phase. Usually solitary and harmless, locusts change dramatically after drought is followed by rapid vegetation growth, when [[Serotonin|serotonin]] in their brains triggers breeding and gregarious behavior. They form bands of wingless [[Nymph (biology)|nymphs]] that later become winged swarms, which strip fields and damage crops. Locusts have plagued people since [[Prehistory|prehistory]], and ancient Egyptians carved them on tombs. Swarms have caused [[Famine|famines]] and human migrations. Traditional control uses insecticides applied from the ground or air, though biological methods are proving effective. Locusts are edible and are considered a delicacy in many countries.

American influencer and professional wrestler. He gained a following on Vine and built the [[YouTube]] channel Logan Paul Vlogs, which has over 23 million subscribers. Paul co-founded the beverage company Prime and the snack brand Lunchly, and he was ranked on the [[Forbes]] list of highest-paid YouTube creators in 2017, 2018 and 2021. He has been signed to [[WWE]] since June 2022 and won the WWE United States Championship in November 2023. In 2023 he won his first professional [[Boxing|boxing]] match. In 2017 he filmed himself finding the corpse of a suicide victim in Japan's Aokigahara forest, a notorious suicide site, and uploaded the footage. He apologized, and YouTube temporarily suspended his premium content privileges. He also promoted CryptoZoo, which failed to compensate more than $1.5 million to investors.

Device that performs a Boolean function, a logical operation on one or more binary inputs that produces a single binary output. Most gates are built from [[MOSFET|MOSFETs]] (metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistors) acting as electronic switches, though they can also use [[Vacuum tube|vacuum tubes]], electromagnetic [[Relay|relays]], optics, or fluidic and pneumatic logic. Gates combine into multiplexers, registers, arithmetic logic units and memory, up to microprocessors with more than 100 million gates. The seven basic gates are NOT, OR, NOR, AND, NAND, XOR and XNOR. In 1705 [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]] published a refined binary system that combined arithmetic and logic. From 1934 to 1936, Akira Nakashima, [[Claude Shannon]] and Victor Shestakov introduced switching circuit theory, showing that two-valued [[Boolean algebra]] could describe switching circuits. [[Konrad Zuse]] built electromechanical logic gates for his Z1 computer from 1935 to 1938.

Statistical model for a binary dependent variable, with log-odds modeled as a linear combination of independent variables. The logistic function converts log-odds into a probability between 0 and 1. Since about 1970 the logistic model has been the most commonly used model for binary regression. Its parameters are usually estimated by maximum likelihood, which has no closed-form solution, unlike [[Ordinary least squares|least squares]] in [[Linear regression|linear regression]]. Joseph Berkson developed and popularized the model, coining the term "logit" in 1944. The model does not classify by itself, but a cutoff value can turn it into a binary classifier.

Part of supply chain management that deals with the efficient forward and reverse flow of goods, services and related information from the point of origin to the point of consumption. The word comes from the French *logistique*, which the Swiss military writer Antoine-Henri Jomini coined or popularized. It appears in English from 1846, and Jomini linked it to *logis* (lodgings). Military logistics maintains army supply lines with food, armaments, ammunition and spare parts, and also moves troops. Civil logistics covers acquiring, moving and storing raw materials, semi-finished goods and finished goods. It deals with movement between facilities, not with material flow within production plants. Logistics accounts for a significant share of the operating costs of an organization or country, and minimizing resource use is a common motivation in all its fields.

Longest river in France, at 1,006 km (625 mi). It rises at 1,350 m (4,430 ft) in the Cévennes of the Massif Central and flows north through Nevers and Orléans, then west through Tours and [[Nantes]] to the [[Bay of Biscay]] at Saint-Nazaire. The river drains 117,054 km² (45,195 sq mi), more than a fifth of France's land, but its average discharge is only half that of the Rhône. Its lower-central valley, often called the "Garden of France," was added to the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage]] list on December 2, 2000. The valley holds over a thousand châteaux, many of them former feudal strongholds, and is known for its vineyards. Gallic rule ended in the valley in 56 BC, when [[Julius Caesar]] conquered the adjacent provinces for Rome.

God in [[Norse mythology]], described by some scholars as a trickster. He engineers the death of the beloved god Baldr and is bound by the gods; his wife Sigyn catches the serpent venom that drips onto him, and when he writhes, earthquakes follow. At Ragnarök he is foretold to break free and fight the gods alongside the jötnar, and he and Heimdallr are to kill each other. Loki is the son of the jötunn Fárbauti and the goddess Laufey. By the jötunn Angrboða he fathers Hel, the wolf Fenrir and the world serpent Jörmungandr. A shape-shifter, he appears as a mare, a salmon, a fly and possibly an elderly woman. He is attested in the [[Poetic Edda]], and in the Prose Edda and Heimskringla, both composed or compiled by [[Snorri Sturluson]] in the 13th century. Scholars have debated his origins, and he is unlikely to have received veneration.

1955 novel by the Russian-American [[Vladimir Nabokov|Vladimir Nabokov]]. Its unreliable narrator, Humbert Humbert, is a French literature professor who describes his obsession with, and victimization of, a 12-year-old girl, Dolores Haze, whom he calls a "nymphet." Fear of [[Censorship|censorship]] in the U.S. and Britain led to its first publication in Paris by Olympia Press. The book received critical acclaim despite public controversy and has appeared on many best-book lists. It was adapted into films by [[Stanley Kubrick]] in 1962 and by Adrian Lyne in 1997.

[[Germanic peoples|Germanic]] people who conquered most of the Italian Peninsula between 568 and 774. Earlier they lived near present-day Hamburg and then along the [[Danube]], near what is now Austria, Slovenia and Hungary. Under King Alboin they invaded Italy in 568, and by late 569 they had conquered northern Italy except Pavia, which fell in 572. They established a kingdom in the north and center of the peninsula that reached its height under Liutprand in the 8th century. In 774 the Frankish king [[Charlemagne]] conquered it and integrated it into the Frankish Empire. Lombard nobles continued to rule southern Italy until the [[Normans]] conquered them in the 11th century. The region of [[Lombardy]] takes its name from them. Scholars generally accept that the name means "long beards."

Administrative region of northern [[Italy]], with about 10 million people, the most populous region in Italy. It covers 23,844 km² (9,206 sq mi) between the [[Alps]] and tributaries of the Po River. Its capital, [[Milan]], has the largest metropolitan area in Italy. The region produces about one-fifth of national gross domestic product and has 1,501 municipalities, more than any other Italian region. Of Italy's 58 [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Sites]], 11 are in Lombardy. The region takes its name from the [[Lombards]], who arrived in 568 and made Pavia their capital.

Series of crossings of the [[River Thames|Thames]] between the [[City of London]] and Southwark since Roman times. The first was a timber bridge built around AD 50 by the Roman founders of London. The medieval stone bridge carried homes and businesses for centuries and was replaced by a 19th-century stone-arched bridge. The current bridge, a concrete and steel box girder structure, was opened by [[Elizabeth II|Queen Elizabeth II]] on March 17, 1973. The 19th-century bridge was sold in 1968, and its granite facing was moved to Lake Havasu City, Arizona. London Bridge appears in the nursery rhyme "London Bridge Is Falling Down" and in *The Waste Land* by [[T. S. Eliot]].

City in southwestern [[Ontario]], Canada (pop., 2021: 422,324), at the confluence of the Thames and North Thames rivers. John Graves Simcoe named it in 1793 after the [[London|English city]] and river, when he proposed the site as the capital of Upper Canada. It is the largest municipality in southwestern Ontario, and its metropolitan area of 543,551 makes it Canada's 11th-largest. The city is a regional center for health care and [[Education|education]], home to the University of Western Ontario and three major hospitals. Its economy also includes [[Manufacturing|manufacturing]], financial services and [[Information technology|information technology]]. London lies about 200 km (120 mi) from both [[Toronto]] and [[Detroit]].

Public research university in [[London|London]], England, commonly known as LSE, specializing in the social sciences. It was founded in 1895 by Fabian Society members Sidney and Beatrice Webb, Graham Wallas and [[George Bernard Shaw]]. It joined the University of London in 1900 and became a university in its own right within it in 2022. It had under 13,000 students in 2023/24 and an income of £548.2 million in 2024/25. The British Library of Political and Economic Science is one of the world's largest libraries devoted to the economic and social sciences. Since 1990 the school has educated 24 prime ministers or presidents, and since its founding over 40 world leaders and 21 Nobel laureates have taught or studied there.

Global stock exchange in the [[City of London]], one of the world's oldest continuously operating exchanges. Founded in 1801, it has been run since 2007 by the London Stock Exchange Group, a constituent of the FTSE 100 index. Its Main Market serves established companies, and the Alternative Investment Market serves smaller, high-growth firms; more than 1,900 companies from over 60 countries are listed. As of mid-2025, its total market capitalization was about US$5.9 trillion. Its origins lie in the Royal Exchange, opened by [[Elizabeth I|Queen Elizabeth I]] in 1571 and rebuilt after the [[Great Fire of London]] in 1669. Barred from the Royal Exchange, stockbrokers traded from coffee houses, where John Castaing began publishing prices in 1698. A 1697 Act of Parliament penalized unlicensed brokering. Despite challenges after [[Brexit]], the exchange regained its position as Europe's largest stock market by total value in 2024 and 2025. As of 2025, London also had the world's largest concentration of mining capital, about US$600 billion, roughly 13% of the global mining market.

[[Rapid transit|Rapid transit]] system serving [[Greater London]] and parts of the adjacent home counties. Known as the Tube, it has 11 lines, 272 stations and about 250 miles (400 km) of track, managed by Transport for London. Only 45% of the network is underground; its nickname comes from its deep-level circular [[Tunnel|tunnels]]. The network began with the Metropolitan Railway, which opened on January 10, 1863, as the world's first underground passenger railway, using gas-lit carriages hauled by steam locomotives. The City and South London Railway pioneered underground electric traction when it opened in 1890. The lines were consolidated as London Transport in 1933. The network carried over 1.2 billion passenger journeys in 2024–25. Harry Beck's schematic Tube map, designed in 1931, became a global design icon.

Unpleasant [[Emotion|emotional]] response to perceived or actual social isolation. Transient loneliness is generally seen as an adaptive response that motivates people to seek connection, much as hunger motivates eating. Chronic loneliness is linked to obesity, [[Substance use disorder|substance use disorder]], depression, [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular disease]], high blood pressure and high cholesterol. Causes include systemic issues, genetic inheritance, cultural factors, lack of meaningful relationships, significant loss and excessive reliance on passive technologies, particularly the [[Internet]]. About one in six people worldwide experiences significant long-term loneliness, and adolescents report the highest levels. Therapy and antidepressants are medical treatments; social approaches include [[Exercise|exercise]], group activities, reconnecting with friends and owning [[Pet|pets]]. Loneliness has been a theme since the [[Epic of Gilgamesh]], and some academics have called it an epidemic, including former U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy.

Coastal city in southeastern Los Angeles County, [[California|California]]. It is the 44th-most populous city in the United States, with 450,469 residents in 2025, and the second-most populous in Los Angeles County. Incorporated in 1897, it lies about 20 miles (32 km) south of downtown [[Los Angeles]] and sits over an oilfield. The [[Port|Port]] of Long Beach is the second-busiest container port in the United States. Attractions include the permanently docked RMS Queen Mary, the Aquarium of the Pacific and the Grand Prix of Long Beach auto race. California State University, Long Beach, is one of the largest universities in California.

Health problems that persist or develop after an initial [[COVID-19|COVID-19]] infection with SARS-CoV-2. Symptoms can last weeks, months or years and are often debilitating, and their causes are not understood. Common symptoms include fatigue, memory problems, shortness of breath and [[Sleep disorder|sleep disorder]]. Symptoms often worsen after mental or physical effort, a process called post-exertional malaise, and overlap heavily with [[Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome|ME/CFS]]. The [[World Health Organization]] defines it as starting three months after the initial infection, while other agencies start the count at four weeks. As of 2025, prevalence was estimated at about 6–7% of adults and about 1% of children. No validated effective treatments exist, and management depends on symptoms. Globally, over 400 million people have experienced it, and it may cause a loss of 1% of the world's [[Gross domestic product|gross domestic product]].

Densely populated island in southeastern [[New York (state)|New York State]], extending eastward into the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. It is about 120 miles (190 km) long, up to 23 miles (37 km) wide and about 1,400 square miles (3,600 km²) in area. Glacial processes during the [[Pleistocene]] shaped its terminal moraines and outwash plains. Its four counties are Kings (Brooklyn), [[Queens]], Nassau and Suffolk; Kings and Queens are boroughs of [[New York City]]. As of July 1, 2025, the four counties had an estimated 7,957,174 residents, making Long Island the most populous island in any U.S. state or territory. Its economy includes health care, finance, manufacturing and biotechnology.

Military retreat by the [[Chinese Communist Party]] and Red Army during the [[Chinese Civil War]], from October 1934 to October 1935. About 100,000 troops left the Jiangxi Soviet for a new headquarters in Yan'an, Shaanxi, a journey of about 10,000 km (6,200 miles). Only about 8,000 survived. Pursued by the [[Kuomintang]] under [[Chiang Kai-shek]], the army crossed mountains, rivers and blockades. At the Zunyi Conference in January 1935, [[Mao Zedong]] became de facto leader. Official Chinese histories later presented the march as an epic of endurance, while critics stress its heavy losses.

[[Track and field|Track and field]] event in which athletes combine speed, strength and agility to leap as far as possible from a takeoff point. The event dates to the [[Ancient Olympic Games]] and has been a men's Olympic event since 1896 and a women's since 1948. Jumps are measured perpendicular from the foul line to the nearest break in the sand, so competitors take off as close to the line as possible. In major competitions, the best eight after three trials receive three more attempts, and the longest valid jump wins. Tailwinds above 2 m/s (4.5 mph) do not count for records. In 2025 World Athletics began testing a wider 40-centimeter takeoff zone instead of the traditional board, to reduce invalid attempts, which had reached around 30%. The men's world record of 8.95 meters was set by Mike Powell in 1991 at the World Championships in [[Tokyo]].
